title: What will $100 buy in 24 years?
hook: Prices rise 3% a year. Does your cash lose 3% of $100 every year, forever?

knows: that prices usually go up over time
doesNotKnow: that purchasing power erodes by compounding, not in a straight line
how to estimate how long it takes inflation to halve what cash buys

misconception: 3% a year for 24 years takes away 72% of the value (3% × 24).
objective: The learner can explain that each year's inflation applies to an already-reduced value, so purchasing power shrinks by compounding: at 3% a year cash buys about half as much after 24 years.

claims.text: With constant inflation i, what cash buys after t years, in today's money, is cash / (1 + i)^t.
claims.source: Prices multiply by (1 + i) each year, so a fixed sum buys 1/(1 + i) as much each year. Standard, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, chapter 'Measuring the Cost of Living' (chapter numbers vary by edition).

claims.text: At 3% a year for 24 years, $100 buys what about $49 buys today.
Losing a flat $3 a year would leave $28 after 24 years; that straight-line answer is wrong because each year's 3% applies to a smaller value.
At 3%, the first year takes about $2.91 of the $100's buying power; year 24 takes about $1.48.
Rule of 72: 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years is a rough estimate of the time for 3% inflation to halve what cash buys.
claims.source: Exact halving time ln 2 / ln 1.03 = 23.45 years; 72 / 3 = 24. An approximation.

claims.text: The stage's values at other years and rates (2%, 3%, 5%) use the same formula, e.g. after 24 years: 2% → $62.17, 5% → $31.01.
The lesson is a model: a constant inflation rate, which real inflation is not. The rates are illustrative, not a forecast.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: Prices rise a steady 4% a year. Roughly when does cash buy half as much as today?
recall.why: Inflation compounds, so halving takes about 72 ÷ 4 = 18 years (exactly about 17.7), not 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 years as a straight line would suggest.
